strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful controlled comparison in which architectures and hyperparameters are held fixed while only the tensor basis (spherical vs. irreducible Cartesian) is varied (Tables 1–2). This directly addresses a gap in the literature, since prior Cartesian models (TensorNet, ICT potential, TACE, HotPP, CACE, CAMP) were never benchmarked against spherical counterparts under matched conditions.

The theoretical construction is coherent: defining the Cartesian-3j symbol as a contraction of Wigner-3j symbols with path matrices (Eq. 5), and deriving Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan coefficients (Eq. 6), provides a clean analogue to the spherical machinery and allows precomputed product bases in Cartesian space, addressing a limitation noted in ICT potential and TACE.

The paper is honest about limitations, including the curse of dimensionality for high-rank Cartesian tensors, the lack of operator-fusion kernels (oeq/cueq analogues), the exponential growth of precomputed coefficients, and the fact that TACE-v1-OAM-M does not reach SOTA. The design-principles section (linear layers, edge-level avoidance of Cartesian-3j, gate nonlinearity) is informative.

Code release of the Cartesian-3j symbols, generalized CG coefficients, Cartesian harmonics, precomputed product bases, ICTD and ICTP is a concrete community resource, and training details (Appendix D) and architecture equations (Appendix C) are reported.
weaknesses: The reference list is systematically corrupted: many entries have incorrect years (e.g., Coope et al. is 1965 not 2023; Larsen et al. is 2017 not 2025; Paszke et al. is 2019 not 2025; Shao et al. is 2025 not 2024; Batatia et al. 2025c is listed as 2024; Kovács et al. 2021/2023 are swapped). This is not cosmetic—it undermines verifiability and suggests the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

The paper appears to have missing or unrendered figures (the running text 'Irreducible Cartesian Tensor Product and Contraction' appears repeatedly where figures likely belong), and several equations and tables are garbled or dense to the point of being hard to parse (e.g., Tables 1–2 have mismatched headers and unreadable entries).

Novelty over existing work is incremental. The Cartesian-3j is essentially a basis transformation of the Wigner-3j (Eq. 5) and the generalized CG coefficients are the Cartesian analogue of MACE's construction; the framework builds directly on Shao et al. (2025) ICTD matrices and Zaverkin et al. (2024). The contribution is best described as engineering unification rather than a fundamentally new theoretical result.

The central empirical claim—that direct Cartesianization yields comparable accuracy but worse compute/memory scaling—is a negative result, and the paper does not clearly demonstrate a setting in which the Cartesian basis is preferable. The TACE-v1-OAM-M F1 (0.889) and κSRME (0.173) are competitive but not SOTA (eSEN-30M-OAM: 0.925/0.170), and the authors attribute this to the absence of kernel fusion rather than to a property of the basis, which weakens the motivation.

The contraction decomposition results (Section 4.3, Table 7) are presented as 'empirical observations' with no general formula or proof; the authors explicitly state they have not found a general decomposition. This is a significant gap for a paper whose central object is the irreducible Cartesian tensor contraction, since practitioners cannot reliably construct higher-rank contractions without such a rule.

No multiple random seeds are used in any experiment (explicitly acknowledged in Table 1/2 footnotes), so the accuracy-parity claims between spherical and Cartesian models rest on single runs and cannot be statistically distinguished from noise. The 3BPA differences in several cells (e.g., NequIP 64(64)-3-3-5: E 4.9 vs 4.2, dihedral E 12.0 vs 17.5) are large enough that seed variance could plausibly explain them.

The 'first controlled comparison' claim is overstated: MACE's e3nn dependency restriction was removed to enable higher-order Wigner-3j (footnote b), which is a non-trivial architectural change, and the Cartesian models add gates and normalization choices that are not always identical to their spherical counterparts.

The Matbench Discovery comparison in Table 3 mixes models trained on different datasets (OAM vs OMAT24 vs MPtrj) and different parameter budgets without controlling for data, so the 'competitive' framing is not a clean apples-to-apples comparison.

strengths: Provides a systematic framework for irreducible Cartesian tensors (Cartesian-3j, Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, ICTP, and a principled ICTC implementation), and extends e3nn to support these operations, which could serve as reusable infrastructure for the community.

The experimental design of holding architecture and hyperparameters fixed while changing only the tensor basis (ST vs. ICT) is a principled way to isolate the effect of the representation, and it is clearly described.

The limitations section is honest: it explicitly states that Cartesianization does not currently outperform spherical models, that higher truncations are infeasible without operator fusion, and that pure-PyTorch implementations have higher memory usage.
Code release and detailed training hyperparameters (Appendix D) support reproducibility of the empirical setup.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: the Cartesian-3j symbol in Eq. (5) is simply a change of basis of the Wigner-3j symbol via path matrices (C^(l3) · Wigner3j · C^(l1) · C^(l2)). Since path matrices and ICTD matrices are already established (Shao et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026), the 'new' symbol is largely a reformulation of known mathematics rather than a new theoretical result, and no genuinely new capability is unlocked beyond what ICTD/path-matrix machinery already provides.

The central empirical claim — that Cartesian models achieve 'accuracy comparable to' spherical counterparts — rests on single-seed runs. The paper states 'We did not test multiple random seeds as the purpose was merely to verify the correctness of our theory,' so no error bars or variance are reported. Without this, the 'comparable accuracy' conclusion is not statistically established, and small differences (e.g., Table 2) are uninterpretable.

No practical advantage is demonstrated. Tables 1 and 2 show Cartesian variants are at best equal in accuracy and consistently worse in speed and memory (some configurations OOM). Table 3 shows TACE-v1-OAM-M is competitive but not SOTA, and the authors concede this is due to missing kernel fusion. The net scientific yield is essentially negative, which does not support the strong framing ('foundational,' 'best-practice paradigm').

Serious presentation/naming confusion: the authors' model is named 'TACE-v1-OAM-M'/'TACE-v1-OMAT24-M,' yet TACE is introduced in Section 2 as prior work by Xu et al. (2026). The relationship between the authors' contribution and TACE is never clarified, which is highly misleading. The title ('A Cartesian-3j Framework...'), the running header ('Irreducible Cartesian Tensor Product and Contraction'), and the filename are inconsistent, and the notation is garbled throughout (e.g., '\mathscr{Z}', '\exists j', and '3j' used interchangeably).

Internal inconsistency between tables: Table 1 and Table 5 report different cNequIP/cAllegro numbers for what appear to be the same experiments (e.g., 64(64)-2-2-4 cNequIP E: 6.5 in Table 1 vs. 5.6 in Table 5), with no explanation. This undermines confidence in the reported results.

Theoretical gaps in the core contribution: the paper admits 'no general formula has been found by us for decomposing the irreducible components resulting from tensor contraction' and instead relies on numerical observations (Table 7). Additionally, Appendix Eq. (11) is stated to be 'not numerically identical' to Eq. (5), raising questions about the consistency and well-definedness of the central object.

Overclaiming relative to evidence: assertions such as 'first controlled comparison,' 'current best-practice paradigm,' and 'establish the theoretical foundations' are stronger than the presented results and analysis justify.

strengths: Introduces Cartesian-3j symbols and Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan coefficients as direct analogues of the Wigner-3j and generalized CG coefficients. This is a genuine conceptual gap-filler: it enables precomputable Cartesian product bases and a clean, principled correspondence between the spherical and Cartesian formalisms, something prior Cartesian works (ICT potential, TACE) lacked.

The controlled comparison is the paper's most valuable empirical contribution. By holding architecture and hyperparameters fixed and varying only the tensor basis across NequIP, Allegro, and MACE, the authors isolate the effect of the representation itself, which no prior work has done cleanly.
A supporting implementation (cartnn, an e3nn extension covering ICTP, ICTC, ICTD, harmonics, and precomputed product bases) is released, which materially helps others build on the framework.
Demonstrates that a Cartesian uMLIP (TACE-v1-OAM-M) can be competitive on Matbench Discovery (F1 0.889, κSRME 0.173), showing the framework is practical rather than purely theoretical.
The negative results are reported honestly (direct Cartesianization worsens compute/memory scaling; the model is not SOTA), and the limitations/outlook section is candid rather than defensive.
weaknesses: The main-text and appendix tables for the same experiments disagree. Tables 1/2 report different cNequIP/cMACE numbers than Tables 5/6 (e.g., 300K cNequIP energy 6.5 vs 5.6; 300K cMACE energy 8.5 vs 10.5; dihedral cMACE 29.0 vs 17.5). For a paper whose central claim rests on a controlled architecture-fixed comparison, two conflicting sets of results for the same run is a serious reliability problem and suggests the reported accuracy comparisons are not stable.

The 3BPA experiments are single-seed: the authors explicitly state they did not test multiple random seeds. Since the central claim is that ICT and ST models are 'comparable in accuracy,' the absence of any variance estimate leaves the comparison underdetermined.

There is a self-acknowledged theoretical gap at the heart of the framework: 'no general formula has been found by us for decomposing the irreducible components resulting from tensor contraction,' yet contraction is described as indispensable. The properties are then supported only by empirical observations (Table 7) rather than proofs, which undercuts the claim of establishing firm theoretical foundations.

The core construction is essentially a change of basis applied to the Wigner-3j symbol (Z = C^(ℓ3) · Wigner3j · C^(ℓ1) · C^(ℓ2)), so the mathematical novelty over existing path-matrix/ICTD machinery is incremental.

The proposed 'best practices' (nonlinearity is crucial for large datasets, avoid edge-feature constructions, restrict ℓ1 ≤ ℓ2, use gates) are largely anecdotal, with no systematic ablation or theoretical justification; the claim that nonlinearity helps on large datasets but hurts 3BPA extrapolation is asserted without controlled evidence.

The practical value is unclear: the final model is not SOTA, and Table 4 shows it is slower and more memory-hungry than spherical baselines with fused kernels (NequIP-oeq, MACE-cueq). The claim that 'the Cartesian-basis variant can be faster' is architecture-dependent (avoiding edge-level Cartesian-3j) rather than a clean basis-level comparison and is not demonstrated in a controlled table.

Presentation is error-prone: the reference list has mismatched year labels (e.g., Batatia et al. (2024) → 2025c; Chen et al. (2024) → 2026; Coope et al. (2023) → 1965), Eq. (6) is malformed, notation is inconsistent (Cartesian-3j vs 𝒵), and there are recurring typos such as 'Cartesian-∃j'.

The relation to the existing TACE model is unclear: prior work attributes TACE to Xu et al. (2026), yet the paper introduces 'TACE-v1-OAM-M' with the same name without clearly distinguishing it, risking attribution confusion.
